title: Judicial reform: Human oversight may become merely formal
desc: Supports supervised assistance and interoperability while questioning high-volume control and emphasizing inclusion beyond faster processing.

kps.k: Judicial AI reform centres on supervised assistance, not the transfer of judicial authority to machines.
kps.d: The White Paper, UNESCO guidance, Canadian Judicial Council guidelines and IBA discussion frame efficiency as subordinate to judicial independence, due process and human accountability. They support administrative, research, translation and drafting assistance while preserving human judgment. UNESCO reports Colombia’s constitutional ruling as a jurisdiction-specific example of this boundary, not a universal legal rule. The central debate concerns how to make supervision meaningful as AI increasingly contributes to reasoning and draft decisions.

kps.k: Deployment and task-level performance evidence do not establish system-wide improvements in justice.
kps.d: Sources describe classification, clustering, transcription, translation and drafting tools as ways to reduce delays and release staff for complex work. The Brazilian case study cites the Supreme Federal Court’s 2018 report that Victor classified five documents in approximately four seconds at 94.13% accuracy, compared with 44 minutes for an employee; these are institutional claims, not independent measurements. The White Paper describes Projeto Socrates’s 25% time-reduction target, not an achieved result. Adoption accounts also differ: the White Paper describes over 140 operating predictive systems, whereas the case study’s 2023 inventory distinguishes 140 projects, only 63 of which were under development or in use. These figures cannot be treated as interchangeable measures of sustained deployment.

kps.k: The main tension concerns whether formal human oversight actually constrains high-volume AI-assisted adjudication.
kps.d: The Chambers guide stresses that Victor and Maria do not decide cases. Depieri and Meier nevertheless question how their classifications, summaries and drafts influence decisions when case-specific use and verification procedures remain unclear. They cite Galileu’s reported production of 1,954 draft decisions in April 2025 and an unfinished Maranhão investigation that reportedly identified fabricated case law and generic reasoning. These examples raise accountability concerns without establishing general error rates or a final disciplinary finding. Their critique challenges the adequacy of supervision, rather than rejecting all judicial assistance.

kps.k: Interoperability offers an institutional reform strategy, but digitisation alone does not deliver coordination.
kps.d: Interoperable Legal AI for Access to Justice presents Brazil as a reference for shared court infrastructure, datasets, models and expertise, especially for courts without technology teams. It reports that only about 1.1% of cases remained paper-based by 2023, while acknowledging that local variations still obstructed exchange. The Brazilian case study adds concerns about duplicated expenditure, limited disclosure and project attrition. Together, these accounts distinguish the promise of coordinated infrastructure from its incomplete implementation. Transfer to U.S. courts would require funding, institutional commitments and adaptation to local legal and social conditions.

qs.a: Interoperable Legal AI for Access to Justice · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Access to justice requires more than faster processing: public-facing assistance faces legal and inclusion barriers.
kps.d: Certifying Legal AI Assistants reports that, among respondents with civil legal problems in a 2017 survey of 1,049 people in Brazil’s three largest cities, only 13% accessed help. This documents unmet need, not an AI effect. The source contrasts the OAB’s opposition to lawyer-free AI consultancy with its provision of OABJuris to registered lawyers. Translation, simpler forms and interoperable service portals could improve navigation, but their availability does not establish that unmet legal need has fallen. Canadian and UNESCO guidance also warn that inaccessible tools and biased outputs could exclude disabled or marginalised users.

qs.q: Subject To Unreasonable Delay,” Brazil ranked 126th out of 142 countries.86 In a 2017 survey of 1,049 people in Brazil’s three largest cities, the World Justice Project found that of the 69% who experienced a civil legal problem in the past two years, 50% knew where to get advice and information, but only 13% were able to access help, and only 55% fully resolved their problem.

qs.q: Following these precepts would ensure judges avoid introducing biases, which can inhabit AI outputs, promote AI tools that are accessible to all individuals, including those with disabilities, and that they do not inadvertently exclude any segments of the population or inadvertently perpetuate bias against anyone, including marginalized groups.

kps.k: Risk-based rules are expanding, but their legal status and enforcement remain uneven.
kps.d: The Brazilian case study describes CNJ Resolution 615/2025 as strengthening audits, risk classification and oversight, while classifying judge-supervised drafting as low-risk. It distinguishes publication, delayed effectiveness and the adaptation period, and questions CNJ’s enforcement capacity. Separately, the Chambers guide reports Bill 2,338/2023 as pending in May 2025; its enactment forecast is not law, and existing privacy, civil and consumer rules already apply. The guide’s sections give inconsistent accounts of ANPD’s proposed expanded coordination role. International recommendations, domestic court rules and pending legislation therefore should not be collapsed into a single settled governance regime.

kps.k: The practical agenda shifts from ethical declarations to funded, testable and continuing institutional safeguards.
kps.d: UNESCO’s survey reports that only 9% of respondents had organisational guidance or training, while 92% supported mandatory regulation and training; these are respondent reports, not a census of courts. Canadian guidance recommends impartial pre-deployment assessments, pilots and continuing review of workload, rights, security and downstream data use. The White Paper adds secure systems, curated datasets and explicit verification protocols; the Brazilian case study calls for accessible documentation, civil-society scrutiny and examination of private partnerships. These recommendations aim to test real-world effects and preserve accountability rather than assume that a human sign-off or published policy makes deployment safe.

qs.q: **Absence of Guidance and Training on AI**  There is a significant lack of guidance and training on AI usage is evident, with just 9% of judicial operators reporting that their organizations have issued guidelines or provided AI-related training.
qs.a: Global Judges' Initiative: Survey on the Use of AI Systems by Judicial Operators · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: Impact assessments should be done on a continual basis to keep up with the dynamic development cycle of AI tools and include projected long-term impacts.
qs.a: Guidelines for the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Canadian Courts (Canadian Judicial Council, First Edition, September 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

vlens.an: The curated academia-and-research sources collectively accept the proposition’s preference for supervised AI assistance, coordinated infrastructure and access-to-justice goals, while materially developing its concern that nominal human control may not amount to effective oversight. Their common reasoning is that deployment counts, digitisation and task-level speed claims do not demonstrate improved justice: meaningful reform also requires transparent verification procedures, empirical assessment, institutional capacity, interoperable systems and attention to affected users. The strongest extension comes from the Brazilian courts case study, which links high-volume drafting and unclear supervision procedures to risks that judicial sign-off becomes formal rather than substantive, while recommending participatory oversight and real-world evaluation. Material variation lies in emphasis: the interoperability study concentrates on shared infrastructure, coordination, funding and socially informed design, but does not directly test high-volume judicial verification; the Brazilian case study directly addresses verification, transparency and enforcement while retaining AI for non-core assistance; and the access-to-justice survey broadens the analysis to unmet civil legal need, professional restrictions and basic digital readiness, treating AI programmes as promising but unproven rather than examining judicial oversight itself.

qs.q: AI can be of great help in non-core   judicial activities, assisting judges with workflow or administrative   processes, but it should not completely replace human activity in   decision-making.

vlens.an: The Chambers guide supports the proposition’s core model of judicial AI as supervised assistance rather than a transfer of adjudicative authority. It presents tools such as Victor and Maria as performing classification or preparatory drafting without deciding cases, and subordinates asserted efficiency and consistency gains to due process, transparency, challenge rights and human intervention. It also links failures of oversight and verification to potential professional or institutional liability. Materially, however, the guide is less critical than the cluster synthesis: it asserts processing and consistency benefits without supplying quantified evaluation and does not examine whether human supervision remains meaningful under high-volume drafting or classification. Thus it supports the proposed boundary and safeguards but does not substantively develop the cluster’s central concern that oversight may become merely formal.

qs.q: Nonetheless, their use must be balanced against the rights to due process and transparency, ensuring that individuals affected by automated decisions have adequate means to challenge or seek human intervention.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence 2025 — Brazil: Law and Practice; Trends and Developments (Chambers Global Practice Guide) · Market & press · 2025

vlens.an: The selected regulators, courts and professional bodies support the proposition’s core model of judicial AI as supervised assistance rather than a transfer of judicial authority. Across the sources, efficiency, backlog reduction and access-to-justice gains are treated as potential or reported benefits subordinate to judicial independence, due process, transparency, verification and human accountability. Their common response is institutional governance: guidance and training, pre-deployment assessment, pilots, continuing impact review, explainability, data protection and clear human control. Material variation lies in emphasis. UNESCO highlights uneven effects and major guidance and training gaps; its Guidelines and the White Paper define boundaries between assistance and replacement while cataloguing prospective uses; the Canadian Judicial Council most concretely operationalises substantive oversight through impartial assessment, sandboxes and continual review; and the IBA grounds the position in rule-of-law and human-rights principles. Some sources claim or report efficiency and access gains more confidently than the synthesis, but none treats deployment or task-level performance as sufficient proof of system-wide improvement. Most do not directly test the synthesis’s central concern that oversight may become merely formal under high-volume AI-assisted adjudication, so the collective position is supportive rather than a material extension. These conclusions apply only to the curated sources supplied, not to all institutions in this professional category.

qs.q: Human decision-making and human accountability, expressed through the work of lawyers and advocates, judges and magistrates, and courts and tribunals is the foundation of law.
qs.a: The Future is Now: Artificial Intelligence and the Legal Profession · Regulators & courts · 2024

elens.an: The curated 2023–2024 sources support the proposition’s preference for assistive judicial AI under meaningful human authority rather than transferring adjudicative responsibility to machines. Their common reasoning is that claimed gains in speed, workload reduction, affordability and access remain potential or initiative-level benefits, whereas risks to due process, independence, equality, privacy, transparency and public confidence require institutional safeguards. They therefore emphasise judicial education, explainability, pre-deployment assessment, pilots, continuing impact review and legal compliance—not human sign-off alone. Material variation lies in emphasis: the UNESCO survey highlights uneven effects, documented fabricated-citation incidents and a reported guidance-and-training gap; the Canadian Judicial Council and IBA prescribe more developed lifecycle governance and accountability mechanisms; and the access-to-justice survey redirects attention toward unmet civil legal need, digital readiness and professional restrictions on public-facing AI. None directly demonstrates that high-volume oversight has already become merely formal, but all reinforce the synthesis’s concern that supervision must be substantive and that faster processing does not itself establish system-wide justice improvements. Because these are selected sources, their agreement should not be treated as evidence of prevalence across judicial or professional communities.

qs.q: Human decision-making and human accountability, expressed through the work of lawyers and advocates, judges and magistrates, and courts and tribunals is the foundation of law.
qs.a: The Future is Now: Artificial Intelligence and the Legal Profession · Regulators & courts · 2024

elens.an:
The curated 2025 sources collectively accept the proposition’s core boundary: judicial AI may assist with administration, research, translation, classification and drafting, but judicial authority, verification and accountability must remain human. They commonly justify that position through due-process, judicial-independence, transparency, reliability and fundamental-rights concerns, while treating efficiency and access-to-justice gains mainly as potential or reported benefits rather than demonstrated system-wide outcomes.

As a time-period perspective, the material builds materially on the proposition by moving from general human-in-the-loop principles toward the institutional conditions needed for meaningful oversight at scale. It identifies concrete pressures on that model: high-volume decision drafting, unclear verification procedures, limited case-specific disclosure, fragmented systems, project attrition, uneven regulatory enforcement and insufficient public scrutiny. It also develops practical responses through audits, continuing review, curated datasets, participatory oversight, shared infrastructure and interoperability adapted to local social and legal conditions.

There is material internal variation in emphasis, but not an overall split. The Chambers guide, UNESCO Guidelines and White Paper are comparatively affirmative and governance-oriented: they stress that systems do not decide cases, assign final responsibility to judges and prescribe continuous supervision. The interoperability source concentrates less on individual verification and more on coordinated infrastructure, funding and socially informed design. Depieri and Meier are more sceptical about implementation, arguing that formal assurances of supervision may not amount to substantive review when AI produces drafts at volume and procedures remain opaque. That source most directly strengthens the cluster’s principal concern; the others support the boundary but investigate its possible failure less deeply. None of these selected sources rejects supervised judicial assistance, and their agreement should not be read as evidence of prevalence beyond this curated corpus.
